On each given day, we blend data by adding the total quoted amount in the order book from both sources for each displayed currency pair. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. For example, a 90th percentile reading for EURUSD indicates that the current depth of book value is ranked in the top 10% of historical observations over the last year. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Spread data represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. records.text: M Idea 14 Banks ABN (ABN NA) Giulia Aurora Miotto, Ned Tidmarsh Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €36/sh (Upside to PT: 16%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: We see a compelling case coming from cost and capital optionality, with clear management commitment to deliver on optimising capital, lowering costs and profitable growth. We particularly like the plans to lower capital allocation to the less profitable Corporate division and committing to distributing up to 100% via payouts. The details provided on the cost plan offer reassuring detail and will leverage attrition and technology to drive savings - we see C/I reaching ~54% by 2028. Valuation : At 1x P/TNAV for ~12.5% 2028e ROTE, and a lot of excess capital, we rate ABN Overweight and Top Pick, given the strong restructuring optionality on costs and capital. We think 2026 will be a key year for delivery. Catalysts: Delivery on targets, in particular costs and FTEs, will be the key catalyst. Risks: Missing on delivery, especially on costs, could pose a risk, given ABN's track record is mixed when it comes to costs, with previous plans on FTE reduction not materialising. In addition, M&A activity could distract from the core investment case, although management's comments that focus will be on successful integration of existing M&A deals were reassuring. Headline CPI has missed in two of the last three prints, with November missing expectations by a wide 0.3pp (coming in at 3.25% y-o-y). Where will inflation land in December? A little higher, we think. Headline CPI, we project, will rise to 3.4% y-o-y, with core CPI up to 3.3% y-o-y. Services CPI, we think, will move to 4.6% y-o-y on the back of stronger travel and hotel prices. RPI, we think, will edge up to 4.2% y-o-y. Much will depend, however, on the price collection period. A later collection period, as we expect, could drive prices higher (temporarily), and perhaps raises upside risks to our own projections. Looking ahead, we see the inflation downtrend largely intact, with headline CPI likely to push down towards the Bank of England's 2% target from spring onwards. Geopolitical tensions, margin rebuilds, and a renewed threat of trade war, however, could disrupt the UK's swift disinflation process. What to expect for December? December inflation data tend to be more volatile given seasonal factors. Indeed, the Christmas seasonal period can have marked impacts on services prices - mainly for things like hospitality, travel, and accommodation prices. records.text: Relative to a counterfactual where the deal stays in place, pausing the EU tariff reduction on imports from the US would generate some limited upside to inflation but avoid the loss of around EUR 5bn of tariff revenue. We expect limited downside to growth, mostly coming from the US reverting back to higher auto tariffs (Exhibit 1, right). That said, in the event of the EU pausing the implementation of the deal, it is possible that the US administration responds more forcefully than with a simple increase in the autos tariff. Counter-Tariffs on EU Goods Imports from the US The second retaliation option would be to impose counter-tariffs on goods imports from the US. During the EU-US trade dispute last year, the EU already identified EUR 93bn worth of EU goods imports from the US that could be targeted by higher EU tariffs. These include agricultural products, aircraft and cars (Exhibit 2, left). The implementation of these tariffs was suspended until February 6, 2026, following the EU-US trade deal. But the EU Commission could let these tariffs be implemented after a non-binding consultation with EU ambassadors. Therefore, the procedural hurdle for counter-tariffs is low but it is unlikely that tariffs on the US would be introduced if the main member states do not agree with the decision. Our estimates suggest that the counter-tariffs would have limited implications for European growth and inflation. Assuming that the tariff rate would be set at 10%, we estimate a 0.06% boost

records.text: M Idea 36 Energy SBM Offshore (SBMO NA) Guilherme Levy Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €30/sh (Upside to PT: 4%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: SBM Offshore should not be viewed as a typical, highly volatile oil services name, in our view. The company builds and operates FPSOs for the oil industry (i.e. ship-shaped offshore oil and gas production platforms). When customers prefer not to pay for a platform up front, SBM also offers leased units, generating long-term, contracted revenues that are fixed and largely independent of oil prices, typically over 20- 30 years. For most companies in the sector, backlog visibility of 2-3 years is considered strong. SBM, by contrast, offers a much higher level of earnings and cash flow certainty, which we believe should justify a valuation premium vs. peers. Based on its fleet of leased FPSOs and FPSOs under construction (i.e. its contracted asset backlog), the company is expected to generate a FCF yield of over 23% in 2026, followed by a sustained FCF yield of around 10% in subsequent years. In addition, as one of the most established FPSO builders in the industry, SBM Offshore is well positioned to capture its fair share of future demand. While we expect a softer oil price environment in 2026–27, oil & gas producers remain focused on the sustainability of their long-term production profiles. A revival of US–EU trade tensions and the subsequent risk-off has done little to weigh on EURUSD with the pair holding up well just above 1.16. This is in spite of tit-for- tat escalation as a Greenland-related US tariff threat to EU states was met by an EU threat to go back to a tariff list prepared last year, and roll out of its anti-coercion instrument to limit US companies’ EU market access. In the past the market has suggested bilateral tariffs are bullish for the USD as the US suffers less economically as an importer. However, we see some unique circumstances suggesting escalating tensions may be bullish for EURUSD. US tariffs on the EU may be perceived as less credible by the market than in the past given the risk that those implemented under the IEEPA are struck down. Even if these latest threats materialise, EU exports to the US as a share of total exports have declined to just 10% (Figure 1). If implemented as stated, our preliminary estimates suggest that the tariffs would shave off around a little less than 0.1% from 2026 eurozone GDP. We also see a number of paths through which the Greenland issue may prove bullish for EURUSD. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 65 KGHM (KGH PW) Ioannis Masvoulas Rating: Overweight; Price Target: PLN 274 /sh (Price change to PT: -12%); Risks skewed to Bull Case: PLN 495 (Upside: 59%) - Risk-reward overview Investment case: KGHM offers a compelling self-help story, driven by meaningful scope for operational efficiencies, unit cost containment, and improved capital allocation discipline. Core Polish assets (66% of NPV) sit on the upper half of the cost curve, offering substantial operating leverage to copper and silver prices at this point in the commodity cycle. Further, international assets (10% of NPV) are performing strongly under the new management, demonstrating the group’s ability to execute operational improvements. For example, regarding the underlying inflation, it states that ‘Japan's economic growth being modest is no longer the baseline scenario, and this has reduced the possibility that the underlying trend in prices will become sluggish,’ indicating a shift from the view held up to the October meeting. First, a lot of EU trade losers remain depressed and under-owned (Autos and Chemicals in particular), with our tariffs basket still down c5% vs pre-Liberation day highs. Second, markets may resist over-reacting this time around, as investors have been increasingly leaning into the so-called 'TACO trade' when policy noise rises but concrete action remains uncertain. Third, the US political cycle also matters. With consumer affordability becoming the central theme ahead of the midterms, the scope for a major tariff escalation looks constrained, in our view. Any tariff pass-through into inflation would also complicate the Fed’s cutting path, raising the probability of incremental exemptions rather than blanket measures. Finally, the Supreme Court’s forthcoming IEEPA ruling adds another layer that may limit immediate policy implementation. So while not dismissing the tail risk of more escalation, we believe any pull-back could end up offering a good medium-term buying opportunity, and stick to our constructive central scenario (see Starting on a high – January Chart Pack, 7 Jan). This week will likely prove eventful again, with Trump expected to travel to the World Economic Forum in Davos. Events in Venezuela and geopolitics could also impact the election (see Latin America: Impact of Venezuelan regime shift, 8 January). We think a victory for the right could bring some fiscal consolidation and help local assets. As this possibility is not yet reflected in local assets, we think the risk–reward is positive for government bonds (Colombia: Entering 2y IBR – Coltes 2035 flattener, 13 January). For FX, the outlook is less asymmetric, as the COP is already trading at the upper end of the REER range supported by the government’s TRs programme and attractive carry. Brazil: October’s elections look binary in terms of Brazil’s fiscal outlook, and investors are concerned about fiscal dominance risks, with debt sustainability issues weighing on inflation expectations. Despite the binary impact on the fiscal trajectory, the BRL faces a positive asymmetry given the following factors: a) our positive take on EMFX amid a lack of USD strengthening, b) elevated carry and c) the BRL keeping a relevant underperformance relative to the rest of Latam (measured since the beginning of 2024). Last year’s tax exemption produced sharp monthly price declines in affected categories (restaurant food, alcoholic beverages, toys, games and hobby supplies, children’s clothing and selected grocery items such as snack foods and confectionery). As those unusually low base year prices roll out of the 12 month comparison, they mechanically push year over year inflation higher. Consistent with StatCan’s breakdown, restaurant prices were the single largest driver of faster headline inflation in December: food purchased from restaurants jumped to 8.5%Y from 3.3%Y, while alcoholic beverages inflation stores also accelerated. We therefore see more signal in the continued cooling of CPI trim and median than in the temporary pickup in headline, while still acknowledging that policy related base effects can keep the 12 month headline rate noisy in the near term. Food inflation remains a notable outlier. Even though grocery prices were flat on the month, food purchased from stores rose 5.0%Y in December, with particularly strong gains in coffee and fresh or frozen beef. Restaurant food inflation has accelerated both because of the GST/HST base year effect and possibly a lagged passthrough of higher grocery costs. Combining food at home and food away from home, overall food inflation is running at 6.2%Y and about 4.5% on a 3M SAAR basis, far outpacing headline CPI. Energy, and gasoline in particular, moved in the opposite direction and helped restrain the headline.

Further, non-China manufacturing capacity in SEA and South Korea is also expected to build over the next few years. However, reorienting supply chains will take time, and we expect constraints to significantly lessen only post-2030. Safe-harboring to support builds till 2030: The safe-harbor provision offers some near-term relief – solar projects that begin physical construction before 4 July 2026 will be eligible for the tax credits for up to four years i.e. they must commission by 31 December 2030 (Figure 27 on page 14). The V/U ratio, which we only have until November, remained stable at 0.4 (Figure 13). Redundancies remain elevated, even before notifications pick-up in December The redundancy rate rose from 3.8 per thousand to 4.9 per thousand on a non-overlapping 3mma basis in November, although this was down slightly from 5.3 in the 3m to October. Outside of the pandemic, these are the highest rates since early 2014. The elevation since the middle of 2025 is before the impact of the rise in potential redundancies that we saw in December in the HR1 notifications which implies it has further to go from here in coming weeks. Taken together, labour market continues to ease and will do so going forward Today's data reinforces our view that the labour market is easing and that we are now seeing the impact of that come through in wage data. We expect this easing to continue over the next 3-6 months with the unemployment rate peaking at 5.3% on a monthly path (5.2% at the quarterly average), although today's data raises some upside risks to that outlook. records.text: European Economics 19 January 2026 Citi Research 2 In the latest escalation of transatlantic tensions, US President Trump announced over the weekend an additional 10% tariff on imports from 8 European countries – Denmark, Germany, France, the Netherlands, UK, Norway, Sweden and Finland - as leverage over their opposition to his bid to take control of Greenland. These new “Greenland” tariffs would come on top of the existing 15% in place since last summer on a large share of US imports from all of Europe. The Greenland tariff would rise to 25% by the summer if no deal is reached, the President said. We see this new deployment of tariffs as fundamentally different in nature to those announced and implemented in 2025. They are explicitly not intended to rebalance trading relations between the US and European countries, but at supporting territorial ambitions of the United States. We therefore expect that they will meet with a qualitatively different response from the relatively passive European stance of last year. Indeed, Europe has responded with strong clear-bipartisan condemnation and has threatened retaliation. A first meeting on Sunday reportedly agreed on counter- tariffs on EUR93bn of US imports into the EU (over 35% of total imports from the US excluding energy). French President Macron also called for the EU to explicitly consider the use of the far-reaching Anti Coercion Instrument. However, we think this stemmed partly from perceptions of the party’s own shortfalls relating to governance and corruption. records.text: M Idea 2 A$14bn partnership - more than meets the eye GMG has established a European data centre development partnership (GEDCDP) - with its partner CPPIB (Canada Pension Plan Investment Board) - to hold four data centre projects, including FRA02, AMS01, PAR01, and PAR02. The stated end value is A$14bn, across 435MW of primary power (or 282MW of IT load). In this note, we explore the various types/quantum of profits that may be unlocked now that the JV has been put in place. These include: • Development EBITDA - recognised upfront, upon setting up of the partnership, we'd expect most of this to be booked in FY26/27; • Fee income - Developments - the customary 3-5% development management fee (on capex spent) should be earned by GMG throughout the construction phase of the data centres; • Upon completion, Development EBITDA - GMG could choose to sell down some of its 50% stake in GEDCDP, which would result in cash EBITDA, or if it holds onto its interests, there will be positive NTA uplift. In addition, there could be Development Performance Fees if, at completion, the asset's value outstrips what's in the feasibilities; and • Recurring income - upon finalisation of the developments. The exact quantum of this would depend on the final stake that GMG regains in GEDCDP when the partnership is stablised. Tailwinds include substantial fiscal support (larger tax refunds), as the US together with Germany lead a rise in fiscal deficits across developed economies in 2026 (Figure 2). E asy financial conditions following Fed rate cuts and a reduction in trade uncertainty are also supportive. We see this as limiting the room for Fed easing, though still moderating inflation a nd a potentially more dovish FOMC will in our view see the Fed cut rate s once more, in September, bringing the fed funds rate to 3.25-3.50%. While the well-flagged two-speed nature of the US economy creates some risks , we see a broadening of growth as more likely than a slowdown this year. The euro area is experiencing a "two-economy problem" of its own, characterized by both cyclical resilience and structural rigidities. records.text: this week is the Supreme Court hearing on Governor Cook on Wednesday (Jan 21). The administration is trying to block Cook from serving as a member of the Board of Governors, and by extension the Federal Open Market Committee, while allegations of mortgage fraud against her are being considered. Although the hearing this week may not coincide with a decision, a ruling to remove Cook from voting on monetary policy would open the door for any monetary policy maker who voted against the perceived preferences of the executive branch to be removed by being accursed of wrongdoing. That would have far-reaching consequences for the Fed's independence, and create a precedent whereby future White Houses could potentially have a legal avenue to omit opposing votes. The rest of the spending effects will be spread throughout the year. History points to a similar outcome; there have been many cases where income growth in 1Q far outpaces spending growth in a similar way (Exhibit 8 ). Overall, we still expect consumption growth to slow in 1Q, but the fiscal bill, partly through higher refunds, boosts 2026 consumption by ~20bp on net. With refunds only adding a few tenths, we still expect real consumption growth to slow in 1Q due to a few factors: we expect more tariff pass through to price, residual seasonality is a drag, and recent weakness in real income growth weighs on spending in the near term. Still, the extra income from refunds will add support throughout 2026. Overall, we expect the higher tax refunds and changes in withholdings from the bill will add close to 40bps to real consumption this year. This is partly offset by spending cuts to transfer payments within the fiscal bill, which we expect to be a ~20bp drag on real consumption. Studies and surveys show that durable goods, everyday purchases, and vacation spending should benefit. Souleles (1999) found that the largest effect from tax refunds on spending was on durable goods. The anticipation of political noise: The 2026 election cycle is already injecting volatility into Brazil’s macro-financial outlook, even though the formal campaign has not yet begun. Representatives currently holding executive, legislative or judicial roles who intend to run – whether for the presidency, the lower-house and Senate seats, or state governorships – must resign from their posts by 4 April. Party conventions are scheduled for the end of June through to early July, and candidate registrations with the Electoral Supreme Court must be lodged by the end of July. records.text: M Idea 10 boost spending somewhat. Souleles (1999) found a marginal propensity to consume out of tax refunds of at least 35% within a quarter. The paper also found that liquidity constraints play an important role. Other studies done on the responses of consumers to stimulus checks, not particularly tax refunds, have found similar estimates. For example, the BLS found in a survey done four months after Covid stimulus checks were disbursed that households reported spending 40% of the checks. It did not find the same relationship with liquidity-constrained households spending more, but it did find that younger consumers were more likely to spend while seniors were more likely to pay down debt. We expect higher refunds could boost 1Q consumption by a few tenths. If we take this assumption that around 35% of refunds would get spent within three months, then for simplicity let's assume about 15% of refunds received from mid-February through the end of March get spent by the end of March. If we then assume 65% of refunds are received by the end of March and refunds altogether are $55bn higher this year, this would imply a 40bp boost to real consumption (on an annualized basis) in the first quarter. However, considering about 50% of the refunds are going to high-income and older households that are more likely to save and pay down debt, as we describe below, we expect the total consumption impact in 1Q could be smaller than this. These fiscal dynamics stand to influence the BRL, inflation expectations, monetary policy and, ultimately, the medium-term growth outlook. This makes the next administration’s early fiscal decisions pivotal for long-term macroeconomic and financial stability. Our base case incorporates minimal changes to the fiscal outlook, with the main focus on modest spending cuts. The exchange rate is the main transmission channel for inflation: Apart from local price behavior and commodity dynamics, the exchange rate remains a critical determinant of inflation expectations in Brazil. Our estimates suggest that a 10% depreciation of the BRL generates an inflationary impact of about 95bp over a 12-month horizon. In election years, FX tends to react first to shifts in how the market perceives fiscal credibility, amplifying inflation dynamics beyond the immediate election period. FX will be a key variable in determining where 2027 inflation expectations and forecasts will land, thus having an impact on the BCB’s terminal rates in 2026. records.text: M Idea 90 Catalysts: • Strong outsourcing trend continuation: Institutional decisions to outsource their catering facilities are no longer just about saving cost, but also about dealing with a myriad of regulations, consumer expectations, digital/data needs and health/ longevity changes. These are not receding, and with a $360bn TAM, of which nearly half is still outsourced and ~30% sits with smaller players, there is a long runway of growth. Compass said at the FY25 results that 45% of new business wins in the previous 12 months had come from first-time outsourcing, up from one- third pre-Covid, and the value of its pipeline was at a record $3.8bn. The company enjoys structural advantages in scale, purchasing and its sectorisation strategy, and our capex analysis suggests it is generating a ≈strong ROIC (here). Net contract wins were at the upper end of management's 4-5% target in 2H25, which bodes well for FY26. • Steady margin expansion: We see a clear path for steady ~10bps annual margin growth, given (i) Compass's 7.2% FY25 EBIT margin was still 30bps below pre- pandemic levels (all from a 200bps gap in International); (ii) operating leverage (we estimate 1% on net contract gains adds 5bps to margins at contract maturity); and (iii) synergies from the recent acquisitions (~20bps to group margins). records.text: Across these and other indicators, our forecast performance benefited from our use of alternative data, our suite of proprietary indicators, the insights of our equity analysts, and accounting for potential distortions. As in previous years, our monthly core PCE inflation forecasts (100% hit rate) benefited from the detailed CPI and PPI source data that we incorporate into our estimates. Our forecasting performance lagged consensus and our own record for the ISM manufacturing index (44% in 2025 vs. 55% since 2017). While economywide growth was robust in the second half of 2025, our week-ahead forecasts for the ISM index and other manufacturing surveys were often too optimistic (our ISM forecasts averaged 49.1 in 2025H2 vs. a realized average of 48.4). We also had middling performances for Philly Fed, core capex orders, and ADP , with hit rates at or only slightly above 50%, as in previous years. Forecast Accuracy Across Second-Tier Data In Exhibit 5, we perform the same hit-rate analysis for 16 second-tier indicators, which tend to produce small or negligible market reactions. Our 2025 hit rate averaged 64% across these indicators—close to our 62% average since 2017. Hit rates were at or above 50% for 14 of the 16 indicators, with particularly strong performances for unit labor costs (83% hit rate in 2025), auto sales (78%), JOLTS (75%), and core PPI (75%). records.text: ntial transmission capacity expansion is still required to address grid constraints – and building new transmission lines in the US can take more than a decade (Figure 6). Transformer supply chain risk: The US is a net importer of transformers, with imports rising sharply since 2021 (Figure 12 and 13). While domestic manufacturers are expanding capacity, even US-made transformers rely on grain-oriented electrical steel cores, which are predominantly imported from China and Japan, leaving the supply chain exposed. Behind-the-meter solutions still at early stage: Announcements of co-located power supply with data centers have surged in 2025, particularly in Texas and PJM. This approach can help bypass interconnection queues; however, most projects announced to date are megawatt-scale, limited their impact on broader energy shortfalls. We expect these behind-the-meter solutions will continue to gain traction, but not to replace front-of-the-meter grid connections in the near term. Finally, hyperscalers would face higher depreciation costs and need to manage operations and maintenance in-house. Standalone systems may also suffer from lower inertia, which is less of an issue for a centralized grid. Services inflation picked up to 3.3%Y (about 4.2% 3M SAAR), largely on GST/ HST related base effects in restaurants, alcoholic beverages and some recreation categories • We expect the Bank of Canada to stay on an extended pause through 2026, having reached the lower end of its neutral range at 2.25%. Food, alcohol and tobacco (FAT) inflation increased modestly. Energy inflation dropped 1.4pp from November to -1.9% y/y in December. This was primarily driven by fuel falling back into deflation territory (-2.6pp to -2.0% y/y). records.text: Unlike in Sweden, the wage and inflation dynamics in Norway feed into a diverging consumer outlook, where we expect real income growth to decline, and drive consumption growth and domestic demand growth lower in 2026. Along with a weaker consumer, in a clear switch of growth drivers, we expect petroleum investment to act as a drag on growth in 2026, following the less buoyant oil price outlook2 and the peak in development cycles for the big domestic oil projects (Exhibit 8, left). Unlike in Sweden, we expect the fiscal stance to become notably less supportive this year, compared with 2025, providing very little additional stimulus to the economy. Still, the fiscal boost of the previous years should continue to feed through and support the economy going forward (Exhibit 8, right). Consistent with these dynamics, cyclical slack is opening up in the economy, as evidenced in Norges Bank’s output gap and a range of other indicators, and we expect a slightly below-potential growth of 1.4% in 2026, only marginally stronger than the Norges Bank’s forecast of 1.3% and below consensus (Exhibit 9, left). Alongside that, we see the labour market remaining loose over the coming quarters, with the unemployment rate staying elevated compared to the historical norm and averaging 4.6% in 2026, broadly unchanged from 2025. Divergent policy settings are likely across the ASEAN subregion, albeit FX volatility is prompting a temporary pause. FX volatility and housing market concerns remain a challenge for the BoK, while the CBC stands less constrained in this regard, but both share concerns over a K-shaped bifurcation. To be specific on ASEAN, despite relatively limited fiscal support, B ank of Indonesia is likely to delay rate (25bps) cuts until March and July amidst sustained pressure on the rupiah. Amid challenges from sluggish consumer sentiment and infrastructure spending, the Philippines is set for a final 25bps rate cut from the BSP, albeit likely marking the end of its easing cycle. In Malaysia, BNM is likely to pause throughout the year, with a hike expected to be its next move in 2027, as the economy continues to benefit from a global tech upturn. While Singapore delivered another quarter of upside surprise in growth in Q4, achieving 4.8% in 2025 and thereby boosting its 2026 outlook, we see MAS staying put through the year, with core inflationary pressures contained. records.text: M Idea 62 Metals & Mining ArcelorMittal (MT NA) Alain Gabriel, Adahna Ekoku Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €46.20/sh (Upside to PT: 10%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: ArcelorMittal offers meaningful operating leverage to a European earnings re-base without a disproportionate exposure to operating or balance-sheet risk. The company’s European assets are currently operating at ~65% utilization, leaving scope to lift shipments by at least ~3mtpa (~10%) as tighter safeguards and higher import costs improve economics of additional tonnes. This volume upside complements a scenario of structurally higher prices/margins, amplifying the EBITDA re-base in a tightening market. ArcelorMittal’s capital allocation framework suggests that incremental earnings/cash generation under our upside scenario would support accelerated buybacks on top of base dividend distributions, reinforcing the equity upside. Finally, we view ArcelorMittal’s approach to decarbonisation as pragmatic and balanced. The company has been disciplined in pacing its decarbonisation spending, sequencing investments in a way that limits execution risk and avoids exposure to excessive operating or balance sheet risks. In summary, we think ArcelorMittal provides leverage to a structurally improving European steel market, with volume, margins and capital-return upside under a policy- backed “new normal,” as well as a compelling valuation in a full-upside scenario. Baseline scenario and possible hedges: We expect the traditional carry trades – HUF, BRL and TRY funded in USD – to keep offering positive total returns in 2026. However, after a very strong performance last year, technicals look stretched (Figure 3), and high concentration risk could mean the risk of a sharp unwind. Asia or EUR-funded carry trades have also become more popular, given their much more attractive vol-adjusted carry profile compared with USD-funded positions (Figure 2), but these structures will likely be even more exposed to a unwind triggered by an economic downturn or a spike in volatility. We think AUDUSD downside or USDZAR upside look like attractive hedges against such risks, especially into the beginning of the year, when historically consensus trades see sharp corrections (Figure 4). Additionally, we think structuring carry positions through options can offer effective risk management as well as enhancing potential returns. Our FX carry dashboard calculates Sharpe ratios for high carry/vol in liquid EUR- and USD-funded pairs. EURBRL currently stands as the highest carry/vol in the universe here, and owning EURBRL carry through put EKOs rather than delta-one could more than treble risk-adjusted return. As outlined in our 2026 Outlook, a strong tax season could bias the probability of scenario outcomes toward our bull case and KNX remains our #1 ranked stock for 2026 overall, followed by GXO and R with CN and CP rounding out the top 5. In the near term, USD/JPY is likely to move in tandem with Japanese equities. Since media reports on the dissolution and general election, USD/JPY has been tracking Japanese equities, and upward pressure has dominated. With the highly popular Takaichi administration deciding to dissolve the Lower House, the market appears to be pricing a scenario in which an LDP victory strengthens the political foundation of the administration and enables PM Takaichi to pursue accommodative macroeconomic policies. As discussed below, the medium- to long-term picture is not so straightforward, in our view. That said, ahead of the election, signs of mounting fiscal populism are evident, and speculators’ logic is unlikely to change. In addition, overseas short-term investors may be going long Japanese equities with FX hedges in the run-up to the election, meaning that equity moves could translate into USD/JPY flows through hedge adjustments. records.text: EU—Retaliation Options in Response to Further US Tariffs We estimate that President Trump’s announcement to impose a 10% tariff on imports from eight European countries from February 1—if implemented—would lower real GDP in the affected European countries of 0.1-0.2% via lower net exports. EU leaders have responded firmly to President Trump’s announcement, scheduling an emergency leaders’ summit for Thursday (January 22) to discuss potential retaliatory measures. In today’s Daily we set out the EU’s potential retaliation options in more detail. Stalling of EU-US Trade Deal Implementation The first option—with the lowest hurdle—is to pause the implementation of the EU-US trade deal that was agreed last August. The EU Commission and member state governments have already signed off on the agreement, but the elimination of these tariffs still requires ratification in the European Parliament. The EU-US trade deal included the elimination of EU tariffs on all US industrial goods and preferential market access for a wide range of US agricultural goods. But the elimination of tariffs, like other trade agreements, requires approval by the EU Parliament. The EU Parliament initiated the examination of the deal last September, and the US followed through by reducing tariffs on European auto exports to the US from 27.5% to 15%, as stated in the deal. records.text: nt Trump has stated that Greenland is a matter of national security for the US. As the Artic ice retreats, its routes become more navigable, opening up shorter and faster routes between Asia, Europe and North America, and effectively leaving Greenland in a position to become an important maritime hub. China’s and Russia’s expansions in the Artic also are also perceived as a threat, and Greenland’s strategic geographical position would become key for monitoring and deterrence strategy. Beyond defense, there’s a commodities angle to it too. Greenland offers oil reserves but more importantly rare earth mineral resources, key for the AI race. Greenland is estimated to hold approximately 36m tonnes of rare earths, though much less is currently considered ‘proven and economically recoverable’ (GEUS, 2023). In 2024, the US Geological Survey estimates Greenland holds 1.5 million tonnes of rare earth minerals available for extraction in Greenland (US Geological Survey, 2024). While still small compared to China’s estimated 44m tonnes, it would allow the US to almost double its reserves. If the US’ intentions are indeed about national security, then the most likely outcome of the increased pressure on Denmark and Europe for Greenland should be de-escalation and a deal that allows the US to extract rare earths, and forces NATO countries to step up their defence efforts in the island. These factors, combined with low allocations among discretionary investors, have led to a strong rally in the last few months (the SX5E has outperformed SPX by 4.5% since December). Short-term caution: We do not expect reported Q4 earnings numbers to be widely positive. The context for near-term guidance is also mixed: 1) our economists anticipate German GDP to begin improving materially only from Q2 and activity data still lags in Germany; 2) revenue models project limited growth in Q1; 3) a year-over-year FX drag will continue to weigh on Q1; and 4) European earnings estimates tend to receive downward revisions during this period as analysts assess growth in the new year more rigorously – and while we believe the growth outlook is achievable, we expect some volatility around it in the short-term . Key themes to watch: ▪ Show me the money (2026): On-the-ground feedback from corporates, particularly in Germany, will be crucial to determine when fiscal spending is expected to feed into the economy in 2026. records.text: M Idea 22 Consumer ABS Carolyn Campbell The expected increase in average tax refunds described above should be a meaningful tailwind for consumer credit performance in 2026. We expect that the seasonality effect seen annually in consumer delinquencies will be more pronounced than average this year in both prime and subprime auto, and in particular stronger than we have seen in the post- Covid period. In auto ABS, this will come at a needed time: we expect that delinquencies will hit all-time highs in subprime auto in January and 15y highs in prime auto. Delinquencies consistently came in at or above the highs for the given month in both prime and subprime auto ABS throughout 2025. For prime auto, 60+ DQs ticked up 5bps in December to end the year where it started: at 0.54%. In subprime, a 26bp pickup of DQs in December pushed DQs to 5.85%, the second-highest level of the year (the highest being January at 5.90%). That sets the new year off on a relatively precarious footing, with prime DQs at the 84th percentile historically and subprime DQs at the 99th versus 20y of history ( Exhibit 36 ). The EU Commission approved last week the first batch of EU SAFE loans for joint procurements to 8 EU countries for EUR38bn. T o sum up, the implications of the new tariff threat is in principle marginally negative for growth in the near term, but shifts the balance of risk to inflation on the upside. Given the new instability of international relations this creates, it is also fair to recognize that the variance of plausible outcomes has widened. This new situation further reinforces our key view that the European economic model is shifting away from export-led towards domestic demand-driven, more resilient albeit not stellar, growth. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 31 Restaurants & Food Distro Brian Harbour Impact to Restaurant Demand Acknowledging both our AlphaWise survey results and conventional wisdom suggest that most tax refund dollars are allocated towards savings or goods purchases, we do expect a real, if modest, bump in restaurant demand this year given the unusually large refund pool (+$40-70B y/y). Companies we cover have noted in past seeing excess demand during higher refund/stimulus periods. The impact of this uplift, however, will differ from prior refund/stimulus cycles because the beneficiary mix skews to middle- and upper- middle income households and seniors, rather than lower-income consumers who are a major restaurant customer cohort. This skew generally favors fast casual and full service, due to demographic exposure and also the fact that they are more discretionary forms of dining typically. Food distributors have broad exposure but the more exposed segments are more profitable for them. records.text: Outlook for Sweden In Sweden, with higher-frequency consumer-related indicators pointing to sustained gains in private consumption into 2025Q4, we upgrade our estimate for quarterly GDP growth to 0.3%qoq (from 0.2%qoq previously) (Exhibit 3, left). We expect this trend to persist into 2026 and bring notably above-potential and above-consensus growth of 2.5%, up from 1.8% in 2025, driven by strong consumer spending and rising investment and supported by a combination of expansionary monetary and fiscal policy. The recovery in real growth would be crucial for supporting a still subdued labour market, with the unemployment rate increasing to 8.8% in 2025Q3. As we adopt slightly more conservative assumptions on the labour force and employment gains than the Riksbank but upgrade the outlook for employment growth slightly, we see unemployment rate averaging 8.7% this year, down from 8.9% in 2025 (Exhibit 3, right). Under the “fiscal reforms” scenario, the combination of a stronger BRL and lower inflation expectations would allow the central bank to move closer to neutral rates by the end of 2027, in our view. As part of the virtuous cycle that could ensue, lower rates would reduce the debt service burden, further acting to lower the path of debt- to-GDP. Conversely, in a “status quo” scenario, persistent FX weakness and higher inflation expectations could force a slower easing cycle, a higher terminal rate or even renewed tightening to shun narratives of “fiscal dominance” in the country. Given this, we have built a framework to assess the impact of such trends on the FX market. Our dashboard looks at the implications of AI trends on components of a country’s broad basic balance of payments and its readiness to adopt AI. We collate five factors: electronics exports; market share of AI-related raw-material exports; structural FDI shifts; IT sector weight in equity indices; and AI diffusion (detailed overleaf). records.text: M Idea 26 Siemens Energy AG (ENR GY) Max Yates, Claire Liu, Sara Chemello Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €130/sh (Price change to PT: -5%); Risks skewed to Bull Case: €155 (Upside: 14%) – Risk-reward overview Overview: Siemens Energy is a long-cycle business within Capital Goods, meaning products are more project based, so lead time and therefore revenue visibility typically extends to beyond one year. On top of this nature of the business model, two of its three divisions (>60% of revenue), namely Gas Power Generation and Grid Equipment, are facing unprecedented demand, resulting in current backlogs extending to 2028. Gas turbine demand is underpinned by a number of factors: EM coal to gas transition, growing electricity generation demand (baseload) in developed countries like the US, back-up power for the world’s ever-growing renewable energy, and data centre power generation. Investment case: We like Siemens Energy because i) we think it has favourable earnings momentum relative to the Cap Goods sector and the broader market. We think the consensus forecasts underestimate the favourable pricing in the backlog, and MS EBITA estimates are 6% ahead of consensus for 2028; ii) Siemens Energy has a strong balance sheet, and we expect shareholder returns to restart in 2026; and iii) we see a durable gas turbine upcycle driven by Saudi oil to gas switch in generation, the German infrastructure plan, and Hyperscaler spending. Valuation: On valuation, the stock is trading on 11.4

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 29 Retail/Consumer Credit Jenna Giannelli, Roopi Bhangu We expect the 2026 tax refund season to provide a modest tailwind to discretionary spending, with refunds estimated to be $40–70bn higher y/y (roughly $400–700 per filer) due to retroactive OBBBA provisions. While most refunds are still used for saving and debt repayment, the portion that is spent typically flows to durables, apparel, everyday discretionary purchases, travel, and home-related categories, supporting potential incremental demand in 1H26. The benefit is concentrated among middle- and upper-middle-income households, older consumers, and homeowners, rather than lower-income cohorts. Key provisions such as deductions for overtime, tips, and seniors, as well as the higher SAL T cap, primarily benefit taxpayers who already owe federal income taxes, limiting upside for lower-income consumers. As a result, we think refund-driven spending is more likely to support branded and less price-sensitive categories, rather than value-oriented formats. In home-related categories, we think refunds are likely to support repair / replacement spending and provide modest discretionary tailwinds, providing a benefit to SGI, WHR, and NWL, particularly among homeowners. Within apparel and footwear, AS and M appear relatively well positioned given broad middle-income / upper-income customer base & recent momentum, and we think QVC is well positioned given its older demographic. BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH - Takayasu Kudo, Japan economist Rates: Focus Turns to Snap Election Over Jan MPM As noted above, we expect the BoJ to maintain the status quo in its monetary policy at the January 2026 MPM. In our view, BoJ Governor Ueda is unlikely to provide any hints regarding the timing of the next rate hike. In addition, we do not expect him to mention any triggers for conducting ad hoc bond‑buying operations or funds‑supplying operations against pooled collateral to offset the recent rise in yen rates. Thus, the market’s focus is likely to be more on the upcoming snap election. Prime Minister Takaichi is expected to dissolve the Lower House on January 23, the same day as the January MPM. Overall, the risk for yen rates remains skewed to the upside. Total fiscal expenditure for FY2026 may increase further, and the planned JGB auction issuance is unlikely to be reduced. Given the planned reduction in long-end issuance and the increase in the medium-term sector, the market may express fiscal concerns through flatteners rather than steepeners (see Japan Rates Watch: Special Deficit-Financing Bonds issuance may halt, but net JGB supply still set to rise 15 January 2026). - Tomonobu Yamashita,

records.text: M Idea Goodman Group | Asia Pacific Could double its money GMG's European data centre JV, established in Dec-25 with CPPIB, has impact that spans beyond securing a funding partner. We explore the front-end and back-end profits that may have been unlocked. Generating A$4.5bn of value/profit, from a A$1.95bn commitment: conservatively, that is what we think GMG will have recognised upon completion of all the assets in its European data centre JV (GEDCDP) in 4-5 years. The market is perhaps under-appreciating the significance of this. Furthermore, GMG's data centre pipeline spans c.4.5GW, and this European JV is merely 471MW of it. The A$4.5bn of value/profit could manifest in various forms: upfront income from sale of land into the JV, development profit (could hypothetically generate c.A $3bn of cash income, if GMG's entire stake is divested, albeit we think this unlikely), asset valuation uplift, development promotes/performance fees, plus future recurring income. In this note, we illustrate the possible quantum of each component. To be clear, GEDCDP has estimated capex of c.A$8.1bn, of which A$3.9bn will be funded 50/50 by GMG/CPPIB, and the remaining A$4.2bn via debt, resulting in gearing of c.30% (of the anticipated c.A$14bn end value of the assets). The partnership spans four sites and total power of 435MW, with another 36MW of secured power to be potentially added (at PAR02). What's next? We like GMG - we have a A$41.50 PT. We also see potential for updated longer-dated guidance: Given the direction of travel of UK network project costs since the last long-dated guidance in May 2024, we see upside risk to the existing 6-8% EPS CAGR guidance range if longer-dated guidance is presented. Risks: Key risks to our base case include: 1. Supply chain bottlenecks: The acceleration in annual network spending across the sector will most likely come with unusual supply chain constraints that the sector has not been used to managing with slower capex growth. In a bear case scenario, we could see the growth profile of capex softened and elongated over a longer period. 2. Customer affordability: The increase in annual T&D capex across the decade ultimately passes through to customers. However, we also note that T&D infrastructure investments have an offsetting benefit in customer bills of debottlenecking the power system to remove localized tightness in supply/ demand, reduce curtailment costs and lower balancing costs. We estimate UK Retail tariffs increase ~5% to end decade, with network fees increasing from ~40% of bill to ~55%. 3. Energy policy changes: Given T&D capex is a response to energy policy for more green electricity generation and a transition within energy demand to electricity, there is potential policy risk to the outlook. In Exhibit 2 below, we show Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates for how much each of these provisions will cost for fiscal year 2026. Since disbursements were not made last year, the "2026" costs are including both the costs for fiscal years 2025 and 2026. In order to figure out how much this should boost tax refunds, we need to make assumptions about the magnitude of each of these. We expect just these new fiscal provisions to boost refunds this year by $40-60bn, and other normal variations in refunds bring our expected range to $40-70bn. In total, the fiscal year 2025 and 2026 benefits from these provisions total $115bn. We expect about 35-55% of the 2026 costs below are due to retroactive 2025 payments and thus will be distributed through tax refunds. records.text: That said, the US firms selling services into the EU have substantial market power, especially in digital services. This implies that European consumers would find it difficult to substitute away from services imports from the US and would likely need to shoulder a significant share of the services tariff. However, the ACI would also allow the EU to take broader retaliatory steps against US services companies, including an increase in the digital services tax (DST), investment restrictions or “buy Europe” clauses in procurement (such as defence). A Multi-Pronged Retaliation Approach While the uncertainty around President Trump’s tariff announcement remains very high, the firm and uniform response of EU leaders suggests that retaliation is more likely than last year if Trump decides to move forward with a 10% tariff on February 1. At the same time, we would expect the EU’s retaliation approach to proceed gradually to leave room for de-escalation. We therefore expect the EU to start by pausing the implementation of the EU-US trade deal and readying counter-tariffs to be implemented shortly after any US tariff increases. Sweden and Norway faced a challenging 2025, shaped by pronounced n macroeconomic uncertainty and global trade tensions, and idiosyncratic domestic cyclical dynamics. Looking ahead to 2026, we see Riksbank keeping rates unchanged amid a notable cyclical upturn but below-target inflation, and expect Norges Bank to proceed with easing only gradually as inflation remains stubborn. The recently announced Greenland-related US tariff presents a downside risk to our growth forecast in both economies. Sweden’s 2026 outlook is characterised by a consumer-led upswing reinforced n by an unusually supportive policy mix. We expect the historical fiscal package to boost growth by 0.5pp and lower inflation notably below target in 2026. We forecast GDP to grow by 2.5% (from 1.8% in 2025), primarily driven by strong consumer spending and increasing investment. Although the labour market faces ongoing pressure, we expect the unemployment rate to gradually edge down, averaging 8.7% in 2026, a slight improvement from 2025. While we see Riksbank firmly on hold throughout the year, we think the next move is more likely to be a cut rather than a hike. In Norway, the 2026 macro mix will likely turn more challenging as disinflation n continues only slowly and growth drivers fade. Softer real income dynamics should weigh on consumption and domestic demand into 2026, while the growth baton also shifts away from petroleum investment amid a less buoyant oil price backdrop and maturing project cycles. records.text: nior deduction. DRI has already acknowledged potential stimulus-related demand upside. TXRH and CAKE both draw from middle- to upper-middle income suburban households which are, in our view, likely to be the most reactive to incremental refunds. BLMN and EAT sit in similar demographic territory and should see moderate benefits. Food Distributors: While CHEF stands out as the most direct beneficiary given its outsized exposure to independents and full service operators, the broader food distributor landscape could still see some lift. The Big 3 serve a broad cross section of restaurants but generate more profit from independents, which skew full service, and less from chain QSRs. Quick Service Restaurants are more convenience driven and habitual and perhaps less a focus for refund dollars. They also skew more low end compared to other segments. With that said, a few concepts with more mixed exposure or discretionary use cases with a group focus could see isolated gains as a result of higher tax refunds: DPZ, given its family and group occasion orientation, and WING, which also participates in group dining and sports driven events. Fast Casual and Beverage could benefit to some extent. Higher-income and geographic exposure may help here, though they are not as occasion driven as full service. SHAK combines higher income, coastal, and urban guests, and a more indulgent occasion that could benefit. Beverage (SBUX, BROS, BRCB) is relatively habitual but a treat for some use cases

A June 2025 Texas law authorizes grid operators to disconnect data centers during periods of system stress. New York has proposed clean-energy procurement requirements (March 2025) designed to ensure operators use clean power to cover at least some of their load. In December 2025, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued an order directing grid management firm PJM Interconnection to develop new rules for co-location of generation with load (including data centers) within 60 days. The order requires co-located load to cover the cost of essential grid upgrades and reliability services. We expect this to be extended beyond PJM. Voluntary initiatives gain traction: In Sustainable AI: Data centers take the lead on push for clean power, dated 14 October 2025, we noted 13 companies (10 US- based) – representing roughly 45% of global data center capacity – had committed to match 100% of their electricity consumption with clean power by 2030 (see Figure 4). Natural gas will remain essential for US data center load growth in the near term, but we expect ambitious voluntary corporate targets to accelerate a portfolio approach – combining power purchase agreements (PPAs), green-tariff programs and on-site generation – that steadily increases clean-power offtake. Experian’s core dataset includes mainly personal information, credit account data (loans, credit cards, payment history, limits, balances), the vast majority of which is confidential data that comes from banks, lenders, courts and utility companies; it is not publicly available and is only shared with authorised parties (lenders, landlords, etc.) under strict regulations (e.g. GDPR, FCRA). AI could in theory replicate a partial view of certain individuals by piecing together court filings, property records, marketing data, and data from breaches, but in our view it would lack the breadth, accuracy, and legal legitimacy of Experian’s dataset, and deliver at best a vague, incomplete and unregulated profile. Experian’s direct feeds from lenders and regulatory legitimacy remain unique and cannot be replicated by AI, which is why Experian’s core dataset remains such a powerful, proprietary and defensible asset.

records.text: November (Figure 5 and 6), domestic demand indicators all disappointed the market. Retail sales growth decelerated further to a multi-decade low of 0.9% y/y from 1.3%, excluding COVID lockdown periods (Figure 7 and 8). Fixed asset investment posted a sixth consecutive month of outright contraction, falling 14.7% y/y in December (Nov: -11.1% y/y), amid falling government bond issuance. In particular, the contraction in infrastructure widened from 12.1% in November to 15.1% y/y in December, hitting an almost six-year low. We think the rapid deterioration in (goods) consumption and investment reflected A) payback from the earlier fiscal stimulus, B) local governments' lack of funding which dragged on infrastructure investment, C) ongoing overseas greenfield investment and weak profit margins domestically that hold back domestic manufacturing investment, and D) worsened property market (Figure 9 and 10) that weighed on sentiment via negative wealth effects with spillover to the upstream and downstream sectors. That said, risks to our 2026 GDP growth forecast of 4.0% are tilted to the upside in view of continued strength in exports and industrial production growth (see China: Exports end the year with great resilience, 14 January 2026), amid the more resilient than widely believed US Consumer (State of the US Consumer: Carts before the horse, 15 January 2026), US-China AI and space race with still solid hyperscalers capex spending and China applying to launch up to 200k satellites

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Executive Summary We expect tax refunds to be $40–70bn higher than those of 2025, largely due to tax cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). The OBBBA included many consumer tax cuts that began retroactively in 2025. These include deductions for overtime, tips, seniors, car loan interest, and an increased SAL T cap and Child Tax Credit. Since withholding tables were not changed last year, consumers will receive the benefit of these provisions in tax refunds over the next few months. We expect these provisions to boost refunds by $40-60bn in total, and accounting for typical variation in refunds, we up our expected range to a $40-70bn y/y increase. Using the midpoint, this would bring total refunds by the end of May to $350bn, +20% y/y. If we assume a similar number of consumers receive refunds, this average refund would be $440-675 higher, coming in around ~$3,500. Higher tax refunds should boost income in 1Q and support spending throughout the year. Typically around 30-45% of refunds are received by the end of February and 60-70% are received by the end of March, but the BEA will incorporate all tax changes in January income. We expect real disposable income will grow at a 4.1% annual rate in 1Q, after running almost flat in 2H25. While refunds (and the bill as a whole) will boost spending this year as well, we do not expect the same immediate jump. At the same press conference, Prime Minister Takaichi stated that, contrary to our earlier expectations, food and beverage items would be exempt from the consumption tax for a two year period. In the original October 2026 coalition agreement between the LDP and Ishin, it was stated that ‘for food and beverage items, the option of exempting them from consumption tax for a limited period of two years would be considered.’ However, in her Diet statements to date, Prime Minister Takaichi had expressed a cautious stance toward lowering the consumption tax rate. Part of this shift likely reflects a response to the new “Centrist Reform Alliance,” established on January 16 by the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito, which proposed reducing the 8% reduced consumption tax rate on food to zero ahead of the snap election. If the 8% consumption tax rate on food is reduced to zero—holding other factors constant—tax revenue would fall by roughly 0.8% of GDP (about ¥5 trillion). Although the Prime Minister has emphasized that the measure would be time-limited to two years, the political hurdle for raising the consumption tax rate again once it has been lowered appears significant. That said, considering the expected increase in nominal GDP and associated revenue gains, we do not see the magnitude of the tax reduction as one that would impair fiscal sustainability. KEY MESSAGES We see fiscal policy as the dominant macro driver of Brazil’s 2026 election cycle. This will likely shape risk perception, FX dynamics, inflation expectations and the monetary policy path from 2027 onward. Brazilian elections often amplify market volatility. Historically, FX has reacted first to fiscal uncertainty, transmitting shocks to inflation expectations and financial conditions. We perceive a binary post-election macro outlook. While a credible fiscal stance may unlock lower risk premia, BRL appreciation, rate cuts and higher growth, weaker fiscal discipline could see an opposite outcome. records.text: Economic Data Surprises, Our Forecast Performance, and Market Reactions in 2025 In this week’s Analyst, we review the economic data surprises of 2025, our ability to forecast them, and how the market reacted to growth and inflation news. How Growth and Inflation Surprised in 2025 With GDP likely having increased just under 2½% Q4/Q4 in 2025, the US economy grew roughly in line with our 2.4% forecast from the start of the year and somewhat above the consensus 1.9% forecast but at a faster pace than looked likely after large tariffs were announced last spring. We lowered our initial growth forecast by 1.9pp cumulatively between January and March (and briefly forecasted recession on April 9) as the White House signaled larger and larger tariffs. After the White House scaled back the largest tariffs that would have been the most economically disruptive in May, we boosted our forecast by 0.5pp. As some of the potential negative effects of tariffs that historical experience might have suggested did not manifest, the outlook for the effective tariff rate began to look more balanced, and activity data surprised to the upside, we gradually raised our growth forecast back to where it started the year. records.text: 11 Fig. 22: US coal power generation retirement by year and region Sources: US EIA, SPGCI, BNP Paribas State of play: The US has phased out 37% (112GW) of its coal power generation capacity since 2015. Coal-fired electricity generation in 2024 was 49% lower than in 2015, according to EIA data. Coal production has also declined materially since its peak in 2008; however, the US remains a net coal exporter. King coal not yet in exile: Trump has issued a series of executive orders to open new leasing on federal land for coal mining, loosen emissions standards and require some plants that are close to retirement to keep running. Over the past two years, utilities have delayed the retirement of 34 generating units (about 16.4GW capacity), partly to power data centers, according to estimates published in October 2025 by Frontier Group. Closures have been put off by a few years, or as much as 20 years. Aging fleet: That said, we still expect a structural decline in US coal-power generation. The US coal fleet is old, with 78% of the capacity in operation for over 40 years (Figure 20), compared to a global average coal plant retirement age of around 37 years. While the pace of phase-down may slow in the near term due to the current policy environment, the long-term trajectory remains downward. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 71 Sartorius (SRT3 GY) Thibault Boutherin Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €300/sh (Upside to PT: 15%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Positioned to benefit from the bioprocessing recovery and macro tailwinds. We expect solid growth for Sartorius in 2026, driven by consumables, with a pick-up in equipment sales representing an upside risk. We believe that Sartorius Group and Stedim are set to outperform in 2026, with more consistent delivery from the bioprocessing business and a recovery of the Lab business. We forecast +9% growth CER for BPS, coming mostly from continued consumable growth, and we assume a continued muted growth for equipment. Sartorius management did not yet see a clear recovery of equipment orders towards the end of 2025, and we believe it is therefore more prudent not to expect a pick-up in equipment sales in 2026 considering the long lead times. In a bull case scenario, a recovery of equipment orders in H1'26 could lead to incremental sales growth from equipment towards the end of 2026 and push the BPS growth rate into the double-digits for 2026. For LPS, we expect the recovery to be slower in 2026 (MSe +3% growth CER) with continued growth in consumable but slow recovery of instruments (~50% of LPS sales). We expect margin expansion, driven by operating leverage and a continued focus on efficiencies (MSe BPS 32% after 31.5% in 2025; MSe LPS 22.5% after 21.5% in 2025, MSe group 30.3% after 29.6% in 2025). records.text: Common Thematic Growth Opportunities Increasing defence expenditure is emerging as a pronounced common theme in both Sweden and Norway. Both countries have materially raised defence spending relative to their previous targets, converging towards higher shares of GDP and signalling a sustained uplift in military investment. With 2025 real defence expenditure up to 2.5% and 3.3% of GDP in Sweden and Norway respectively, both countries signal plans for further expansion3, with domestic production and military spending composition well positioned to take advantage of this surge (Exhibit 11, left). Specifically, in Sweden, factory orders for defence-related industries rose sharply in late 2025, reflecting the country’s comparative advantage in aerospace and land warfare, including aircraft, fighting vehicles and missile systems (Exhibit 11, right). In Norway, the defence industry is more focused, system- rather than platform-oriented4 and is tightly linked with global defence supply chains, which should benefit from the European rearmament, although it is also more reliant on imported content. 3 Both countries have pledged to increase core defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, and total defence-related expenditure to 5% of GDP. 4 Relative to Sweden’s broader array of full platforms (Saab’s Gripen fighter aircraft, submarines, infantry fighting vehicles), Norwegian firms are more often supplying modules, weapons systems, and specialised systems that integrate into platforms. BNP PARIBAS GLOBAL MARKETS APP: SCAN THE QR CODE TO READ OUR PUBLICATIONS ON OUR MOBILE APP The main pathway for lower 10y yields – Fed cuts – has limitations: We penciled a 10y yield forecast for YE2026 at 4.50% – much higher than consensus. Recent developments suggest an increasing chance of yields drifting higher (with steeper curves), and the pathway to lower yields sought by the administration has narrowed. A core part of our outlook has been that the Fed would be able to deliver only one cut in 2026 – vs more than two priced into markets – which should lift long-term yields. However, it’s becoming apparent that even if rate cuts are delivered, long-term Treasury yields (10y and 30y) are less likely to move lower. The mini cut cycles of 2024 and 2025 offer empirical proof. The 100bp mini cut cycle from September 2024 came amid a ‘Red sweep’ in the 2024 election, pushing long- term yields higher (see Figure 1). The 75bp mini cut cycle from September 2025 has also come amid strong growth and dissenting hawkish voices at the Fed, making it less effective. In contrast, the 75bp cut cycle in 2019 saw 10y yields fall in lockstep with Fed rate cuts. Market concerns about future Fed independence have further decreased the effectiveness of recent rate cuts. Yields have moved higher, and the curve has steepened since late November, when Kevin Hassett and Kevin Warsh were reported as front-runners for the next Fed chair position (see Figure 2). Catalysts: A return to using the Suez Canal (after many major carriers like Maersk have been avoiding it) isn’t automatically good news for big shipping liners. While on the surface, it sounds like restoring the shortest route between Asia and Europe, actually switching back can create several operational and commercial challenges for a carrier like Maersk. If many carriers immediately resume using the Suez Canal, a large amount of container capacity (up to millions of TEUs) that was previously tied up on longer routes around Africa could suddenly be released back into the market. This can oversupply key trade lanes and pressure freight rates, hurting carriers’ profitability. We estimate over 2 million TEU of effective supply could be unleashed on to the market if carriers were to resume Suez Canal sailings from the beginning of 2026; a smaller but still meaningful impact if this were to occur later into 2026. records.text: 20 January 2026 Global Economics Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 Overview The start of 2026 has more than lived up to the “Anything But Dull” title of our 2026 W orld Outlook . The global economy started the year amid heightened geopolitical volatility. US action to remove Venezuela’s President Maduro, protests in Iran and escalating tensions over Greenland underscore that international instability is now a structural feature, not a temporary aberration. The US demand for Greenland has particularly amplified transatlantic tensions, with Trump’s tariff threat starting February 1 st raising the risks of a new round of trade war with Europe. We’ll be watching closely how the tensions over Trump’s Arctic Push evolve in the coming days and weeks . Meanwhile, recent Japan- China export restrictions show that geopolitical volatility is not only a US -driven story. At the same time, domestic policy is also in focus in the US. Trump’s decision on the Fed Chair nominee, expected by the end of January, is a key event, while the Supreme Court ruling on Trump’s IEEPA tariffs is another, although this could also come a lot later in H1. Away from geopolitics, the US administration has started the year with a focus on cost-of-living issues, suggesting no slowdown in the policy agenda ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. This comes as the US economy has started the year on the front foot, supporting our above-consensus 2.4% (Q4/Q4) real GDP view for 2026, led by strong growth in H1.

This resilience should allow the BoC to look through near-term growth softness. • Taken together, we believe the BoC has concluded its rate-cutting cycle and will remain on hold through at least Q1 2027, when it is likely to hike to move policy closer to the midpoint of neutral. • A materially weaker growth or labour market outlook would be required to justify further cuts, while stronger-than-expected growth could allow the BoC to normalize policy sooner. Inflation Dynamics The Bank of Canada’s core inflation measures cooled further in December and are now running below 2% on a 3 month annualized basis. CPI median slowed to 2.5%Y from 2.8% and CPI trim to 2.7%Y from 2.9%. On a 3M SAAR basis, CPI median is now 1.5% and CPI trim 1.9%, both near 20 month lows. Three month annualized inflation has been below 3% for six consecutive months, pointing to a sustained moderation in underlying momentum and suggesting further cooling in the 12 month measures ahead. Against this backdrop, we take more confidence that year over year core will converge toward the BoC’s 2% target.

records.text: Outlook for Norway Turning to Norway, wage dynamics should also play an important role. However, unlike Sweden, stronger bargaining outcomes make this a key element for the inflation outlook in 2026. While we expect annual wage growth to decelerate to 3.8% in 2026, below Norges Bank’s expectation of 4.2%, it has surprised to the upside over recent years, making it the key uncertainty for the inflation path (Exhibit 7, left). Under our wage forecast we see core inflation continuing its downward trajectory over the upcoming quarters, with underlying inflationary pressures receding, and see it averaging 2.6% in 2026, down from 3.1% in 2025, below Norges Bank’s forecast of 2.7% (Exhibit 7, right). While food and rent inflation continue to run notably above their historical norms, we expect them to make progress over this year, with more benign cost pressures (both at home and abroad) and further monetary easing providing relief. In June 2025, Fermi America submitted its construction and operating license application to build four AP1000 reactors (total 5GW of capacity). Even if construction were to begin in 2026, large-scale projects typically require close to a decade to complete (Figure 32). In our base case, we expect 3.75 GW from this project to become operational around 2035, based on announced timelines. However, we see downside risks to that view, given the history of cost overruns and delays in recent US large-scale nuclear projects. Fusion on the rise: In July 2025, Google signed a 200MW PPA with Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS), and in 2023, Microsoft committed to a 50MW nuclear fusion PPA with Helion Energy, with delivery targeted for 2028. We expect hyperscalers and utilities to show growing interest in fusion, especially when the regulatory framework and commercial timelines become more mature. That said, we do not expect fusion to materially contribute to the US power mix by 2035. records.text: we extend our Euro area real disposable income infrastructure to Sweden: we use our employment growth projections, forecast the gross operating surplus using nominal GDP growth and project the consumption deflator with our benign headline inflation assumptions. We thus see real disposable income growing by 2.9% on average in 2026, after expanding by 1.6% in 2025 (Exhibit 5, left). While the saving rate dynamics remain highly uncertain, we pencil in a slight increase for 2026, motivated, in part, by “permanent income hypothesis” considerations, bearing in mind that the increase in real disposable income is known to be transitory. We thus see private consumption expanding by 2.6% this year, with risks for an even stronger print if receding uncertainty and a normalisation in food inflation drive the saving rate lower earlier than we expect (Exhibit 5, right). This reacceleration in consumption is critical for Sweden’s cyclical upswing, especially given slowing export growth and only a gradual recovery in residential investment. Given improving activity data but Riksbank’s emphasis on “ample spare capacity in the labour market” and a benign inflation outlook, we continue to expect the Riksbank to remain on hold until 2027H2. We see inflation prints during the first months of 2026 (January-April), and the development of the labour market ahead as crucial for assessing the monetary policy outlook. records.text: ght; Price Target: £30 (Upside to PT: 31%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Compass is delivering double-digit EPS growth from a combination of strong contract wins in a favourable outsourcing environment, steady margin growth, and a boost from acquisitions, which we think will transition to share buybacks. It also has a defensive business model, and its valuation is down to 20x P/E, with 31% implied upside to our price target, with the stock having been held back by the general derating in the quality/growth basket, as well as AI/employment concerns. Supportive valuation: Compass shares were -10% in 2025, despite the company upgrading forecasts and exceeding expectations last year. This partly reflects the weaker USD:GBP (-7%), and partly a derating (from 24x NTM P/E at the start of 2025 to 20x currently). We think the derating reflects the broader sell-off in the quality/growth complex (see charts below), as well as some concerns about US employment and AI- induced office meal demand weakness. However, our work here suggests that even a 10% drop in all office jobs over 5 years would only be a 50bps annual headwind to organic sales, easily outweighed by the 4-5% net contract wins the company is generating and 2- 3% on price. The shares are trading in line with their pre-Covid average multiple, despite the business now growing at a faster pace and having less leverage.

records.text: n the context of the upside scenarios we outlined in our Year-Ahead Outlook. Economic growth has been solid while job growth has been moderate. In our baseline, that tension is resolved by a partial catching up of employment and a partial catching down of economic activity. If growth remains robust, initially, the FOMC will likely stay on hold, worrying that persistently elevated inflation could be exacerbated by stronger-than-expected growth. But the arguments that productivity growth has been picking up are swirling in Washington. A new Chair might be able to convince the Committee to ease despite strong growth, if inflation away from tariffs is not trending up, and the labor market continues to move sideways. To navigate these cross currents, we have the following framework. Short of a Supreme Court decision that allows for a wholesale change to the Fed, we do not see a material change to the Fed reaction function under our baseline forecast. Even if the Court is more permissive, recent political pushback suggests the Fed will not change abruptly. The bigger question is how a new Fed Chair steers the Committee when the economic data are much more difficult to read, especially if strong growth continues with tepid labor markets.

We think Publicis can disprove the AI bear thesis in 2026. See our note, Addressing the Bear Thesis on AI Impact. Our view is that the best source of alpha from ad agencies in 2026 will be from investing in stocks that are able to prove that the AI disruption narratives around them are overdone, and therefore benefit from the rating recovery potential. We see three key elements for investors to look for when stock picking in ad agencies in 2026: 1) attractive entry point, 2) the ability to deliver on or beat growth expectations, and 3) margin upside potential. We see PUB as well placed to continue outperforming its peers, due to: 1) strong product proposition on the back of deep cross-business integration (facilitating the flow of data) and data ownership (via Epsilon offering deterministic data models boasting near 100% accuracy to create audiences and activate advertising campaigns), positioning PUB as an independent viable alternative to data-rich 'walled gardens' in the AI era; and 2) relatively low leverage and strong FCF generation, which provides M&A firepower to continue improving the product portfolio.
