records.text: With sticky inflation but deteriorating growth prospects, a worse consumer outlook, and a less supportive fiscal stance, Norges Bank is faced with a challenging trade-off this year. Given a strong emphasis on fighting inflation and the potential for the fiscal policy to end up more expansionary in the event the Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG)’s performance surprises to the upside, we expect Norges Bank to proceed with easing only gradually. We see them cutting two times in 2026, in March and September, and then one more time in 2027Q1 to a terminal rate of 3.25%. While a later end to the pause is possible (a move in June vs. March), Norges Bank should have a clear understanding of how the wage agreements are shaping up by the time of the March meeting, allowing it to deliver a cut then. The rate outlook remains quite uncertain, and we attach a 50% probability to our baseline, a 30% probability to a slower cuts scenario (with 1 cut per year) and a higher terminal rate of 3.5%, and a 20% probability to sequential quarterly cuts to a lower terminal rate of 3% scenario. Our baseline scenario and probability-weighted path remain below market pricing (Exhibit 10). records.text: • FAI growth deteriorated further, ending the year with a 3.8% y/y fall, the first annual decline since the data series started in 1992. The contraction was deeper than expected (Bloomberg: -3.1%, Barclays: -3%), and weaker than the -2.6% recorded in the first eleven months of 2025. On a single-month basis, we estimate that December FAI fell for a sixth consecutive month, with the decline widening to -14.7% y/y (Nov: -11.1%), the largest drop since February 2020. By firm type, the slowdown was again led by SoEs, where investment plunged 19%. PoE investments declined for the ninth month, declining 15.5% following a 12.8% decline in November (Figure 15). By sector, the decline in manufacturing investment more than doubled, worsening to -9% y/y from -4% previously. Investment continues to shift toward new growth drivers, with emerging industries and upgrades to traditional sectors providing support. For example, manufacturing investment in autos and in railway, vessels, aerospace, and other transport equipment rose 11.7% and 17.5% y/y in 2025, respectively, well above headline manufacturing growth. The manufacturing of digital products also rose by 9% in 2025. Infrastructure investment, meanwhile, fell at a double-digit pace for the third straight month, posting its sharpest decline on record outside of February 2020 (Figure 16). records.text: M Idea 18 Consumer Finance Jeff Adelson Higher tax refunds provide another shot in the arm to already-improving consumer credit quality. In our view, the Fed’s credibility would erode only if the majority of the Board of Governors not only are administration appointees but also exercise historically unprecedented legal authority. The latter might see the central bank alter the operations of regional reserve banks, effect sweeping changes to formulation of monetary policy or deviations in IOER from the monetary policy stance. We see EURUSD topside as the best hedge to this and can envisage a quick 4–6% appreciation should this materialize, similar to H1 2025 (Figure 3). This outcome might also disanchor inflation expectations, which could fuel FX volatility, particularly in GBPUSD and USDJPY. That said, the calculus of the board suggests a narrow path to this outcome. The unanimous vote of the current board (including Trump appointee Stephen Miran) to reconfirm regional Fed presidents in early December suggests little desire for radical change. Furthermore, Chair Powell’s steps after May are not yet clear. If he breaks with tradition by remaining on the board until his term expires in January 2028, only Governor Miran’s seat (whose term ends in January 2026) would be available for President Trump to install a new appointee as Chair. Specifically, its greater weighting towards Life insurance, where we see new business momentum building (primarily protection and capital-light savings), together with its European Retail focus within P&C (where margins are still improving), leaves it very well placed to support earnings growth from here. In turn, we think this can be a catalyst for consensus estimates to push higher. Our forecasts for Generali sit comfortably above consensus expectations for the current plan. Beyond this, we see scope for further value accretion from strengthening its wealth management proposition (particularly in Italy). This could be come a clearer part of the strategy now that the planned JV with Natixis is no longer happening. Valuation: Not only does Generali offer the highest free cash flow yield among the large- cap multi-liners at c.8%, but within this, it also offers the greatest 'optionality'. We estimate that on a normalised annual basis, Generali generates c.€1bn+ of deployable excess cash – equivalent to c.2% of market cap. China Two-speed economy persists China’s nominal GDP growth has remained below 4% for three consecutive quarters on weaker-than-expected domestic demand and negative GDP deflator, which we expect will persist. Strength in exports and IP likely to sustain in 2026 amid US-China AI and space race, and global supply chain reset. Real GDP met target while nominal GDP at near 50-year low (excl. 2020) China's Q4 GDP growth slowed to 4.5% y/y, from 4.8% in Q3, meeting market expectations, and bringing the full year growth to the government target of 5% again. For 2025, net exports added 1.64pp, up from 1.5pp in 2024, contributing to ~33% of GDP growth, the highest share since data became available in 2009 (Figure 1). We estimate consumption contribution rose to 2.6pp in 2025 (52% of GDP growth) from 2.2pp in 2024 with real retails sales recovering to 3.7% from 3.3%, while investment contribution fell to the lowest print 0.77pp (15% of GDP growth) with FAI growth contracting by 3.8%, the first time since data became available in 1992 (Figure 2). Looking at the December data alone, in contrast with the stronger-than-expected export growth which boosted IP growth to stronger-than-expected 5.2% y/y from 4.8% in November (Figure 5 and 6), domestic demand indicators all disappointed the market. Retail sales growth decelerated further to a multi-decade low of 0.9% y/y from 1.3%, excluding COVID lockdown periods

As a result, in this note, we lifted our base case estimates for FY26e/FY27e by 5% and 10% respectively, moving our FY27e EPS to c.€23, essentially our previous (December 8) bull case estimate. On 2 December we wrote: "we identify [TSMC's] 4Q print as a catalyst for the market to revisit assumptions on ASMI." Having seen confirmation of strong growth and capex, we forecast ASMI to accelerate revenue growth on a multi-year build-out for leading edge foundry as the industry scurries to satisfy capacity demand across 3nm, 2nm and 1.4nm nodes. In our view, the company not only benefits from high exposure growth area, but should add double digit share of wallet increases on each sequential node advancement. Our street-high price target of €800, on a 35x FY27e P/E multiple, represents a one-turn premium to the 3-year average NTM P/E multiple – Overweight/Top Pick. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

records.text: cations for the UK Last year, we argued that direct tariffs on the US import of UK goods would have only a marginal macroeconomic impact for the UK. While bilateral trade with the US was down 25.6% YY in value terms (as of November 2025), the spillover into GDP was negligible, with UK growth on track to outperform our expectations at the time. With further tariffs incremental to the already smaller trade balance with the US, we expect the marginal impact to be minor. An additional 10% on UK goods exports would likely worsen the current account by £1.9-2bn per year, with a risk to annual GDP of around 5 to 7bps. Unlike in Europe, we think it unlikely that the UK responds with economic measures. The Prime Minister, talking on Monday, struck a diplomatic tone which suggested that the UK intends to use diplomatic, rather than economic, means to find a resolution. records.text: Global Gas and Power Insights 20 January 2026 Citi Research 2 Price of front-month European TTF futures surged over 30% during the week ending Jan 16th due to a much colder than normal weather outlook and low inventories. Record investment funds’ gross short positions early Jan’26 have also likely exaggerated such upward price movements due to short covering (see our recent note). Markets were increasingly concerned that Europe may run out of natural gas inventories before winter ends. This marked a significant shift of sentiments from late 2025 when weak Asian demand and robust US LNG exports weighed heavily on TTF and Asian JKM LNG markets. While Asian demand remains weak, and US LNG exports stays strong, the degree of coldness and the length of period it sustained have certainly exceeded market expectations (Figure 6). We expect European end-of-March gas inventories to drop to 15-20% full, down from our base-case of 38% full if Feb and Mar’26 are as cold as 2018. Therefore, it is unlikely that Europe will run out of gas storage. Nonetheless, imbalanced distribution of gas storage capacities combined with pipeline bottlenecks mean that some countries or areas may still be at risk of running out of gas supplies. French storage level could be of concern. This note looks at the sensitivity of European gas demand to temperatures and identifies which countries are most at risk of gas stockout. This is also reflected in consensus expectations (proxied by Stoxx 600 Bloomberg revenues, which suggests a contraction of EU revenues in the first half of 2026). According to our scenario analysis, if the EURUSD drifts sideways around 1.16 over the next quarter and EU inflation remains sticky at 2.2% y/y, revenues could start to rebound in the second half of 2026. A depreciation of the EURUSD below 1.16 would help improve EU revenues, in our view. However, if the EURUSD appreciates at a faster pace, the softening of EU CPI could deteriorate EU revenues. Our approach: We use a three-factor approach to estimate SXXP’s reported revenues at the index level. ▪ Price (EU CPI): EU inflation leads EU revenues by three months, according to our analysis. ▪ Volume (EU composite PMI): The volume factor is driven by PMIs, which proxy economic growth. Data suggest that PMIs tend to lead EU revenues by nine months. ▪ FX (EURUSD): The strength of the EUR also affects EU revenues. Our analysis suggests that EURUSD year-on-year growth correlates negatively with EU revenues and leads by three months. Although this share has declined compared to previous years due to ongoing political and economic tensions between the two countries, China remains a key supplier to the US. There is a good reason for the reliance as well – China dominates most of the supply chain, from raw material sourcing and refining to midstream cathode manufacturing and downstream battery production. records.text: Sweden and Norway—2026 Outlook: Diverging Policies, Declining Inflation, Mixed Growth Sweden and Norway faced a challenging 2025, shaped by pronounced macroeconomic uncertainty and global trade tensions, and idiosyncratic domestic cyclical dynamics. Underperforming expectations at the beginning of the year, the Swedish economy started to show signs of a long-awaited recovery amid additional easing towards 1.75% by the Riksbank, which deemed above-target inflation as transitory. Starting the year strong, the Norwegian economy has shown a slowing in momentum, with weaker growth, a deteriorating labour market and still muted sentiment. While the long-guided-for cutting cycle commenced in 2025, stronger-than-expected inflation and moderate growth, supported by notable fiscal expansion, held Norges Bank back from delivering more easing. Looking ahead to 2026, the two central banks face different cyclical outlooks and unusual growth-inflation trade-offs. In Sweden, above-potential growth but notably below-target inflation and a still subdued labour market should see Riksbank keeping rates unchanged. In Norway, as we expect growth to decelerate further but inflation to remain stubborn, Norges Bank will likely proceed with easing only gradually (Exhibit 1). President Trump’s recent announcement that the US will impose an additional 10% Greenland-related tariff on imports from eight European countries, including Sweden and Norway, presents a downside risk to our growth forecast. Last weekend, the Federal Reserve was served subpoenas by the Department of Justice , and the Supreme Court is expected to hear the case against Governor Lisa Cook this week , on 21 January. Her removal is a close call , in our view, and an underappreciated risk. If the court lets it stand, it would likely empower stronger action by the administration against the Fed’s board, which the market would likely see as reigniting concerns about Fed independence and thereby raising the risk of another ‘sell America’ trade (see Fed: Independence in question, dated 22 September 2025). As the prospects for Fed independence have returned to centre stage, our core view on monetary policy credibility remains that regardless of who leads the Fed, policy actions will be determined by the economic outlook, and we do not expect the leadership transition to result in a material shift in strategy. Hence, we do not project any rate cuts after Powell on the back of a resilient economic outlook (see US Fed: Après moi, le déluge: monetary policy in the post-Powell era, 16 January). records.text: 9 Sources: US EIA, SPGCI, BNP Paribas State of play: As of 2024, installed gas-fired power generation capacity reached 505GW in the US, a 15.2% increase versus 2015 (Figure 15). Notably, gas-fired power generation grew by 40% over the same period, implying higher capacity factors. We think this was driven by the introduction of more efficient advanced combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) technologies, relatively low natural gas prices over the past decade, and reduced baseload coal generation. Figure 16 shows gas generation capacity factors ranged between about 40% and 75%, highlighting the flexible nature of gas-fired generation, making it an effective back up to intermittent renewable generation. Turbine supply shortage: US gas turbine supply is facing a shortage, however, limiting growth. Major turbine suppliers have suggested no new turbines would be available until 2028, according to a 1 April report from industry publication POWER. With demand for gas turbines anticipated to increase and tariffs adding supply chain uncertainties, new gas projects are becoming increasingly costly. We would expect projects coming online in 2029–2030 to bear the highest costs (Figure 17). Gas prices may need to rise: Our analysis implies about 4.7bcfd of incremental gas is required by 2030 for increased gas-fired generation. As mentioned above, spending effects are likely to be concentrated in durable goods and everyday purchases such as apparel and home improvement. We expect this demand pivot towards goods to accelerate the already positive restocking developments we have been seeing. Indeed, our latest quarterly Freight Pulse survey showed the inventory situation continued to improve with Ordering net of Inventory remaining in destock mode but creeping back toward restocking territory (best reading since the mid-2024 brief restocking period). We also saw a noticeable increase in Shippers that said their inventory was already normalized or will normalize in 1H26 versus the 2H26 loaded responses in our previous survey, 3 months ago. As such, the OBBBA-driven surge in tax refunds should provide a modest, back-half support to freight demand. While disposable income will rise meaningfully in 1Q, much of the incremental cash flow is likely to accrue to higher-income and older households with a lower propensity to spend, limiting an immediate boost to shipment volumes. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. The above-mentioned points are balanced by two factors: using US military dominance as a negotiating tool could be viewed as bullish USD; and the USD could still benefit from risk-off related to geopolitics even if the relationship is more tenuous than in the past. Since the start of the year, real money appetite for JPY has deteriorated, with flows slipping back into net-selling territory. Although intervention risk is elevated with the yen this weak, the uncertainty surrounding potential snap elections is another source of pressure, keeping JPY vulnerable and volatility elevated. Core goods inflation declined by 0.1pp to 0.4% y/y, reaching its lowest level since September 2024. The volatile semidurable goods component was seasonally weak (-0.2pp to 0.2% y/y), but this accounted for only about one-third of the decline in core goods inflation. The remainder was driven by the less volatile durable goods (-0.2pp to 0.0% y/y) and non-durable goods (-0.2pp to 1.1% y/y), driven by a 1.5pp drop in their combined sequential momentum to -1.0% m/m SAAR (-0.6pp to -0.2% m/m SAAR in 3mma terms). We have discussed at length the overhanging supply/demand issue in container shipping since 2023. During that time, periods of geopolitical turbulence and disruption have propped up the industry, with Red Sea disruption in 2024 and volume front-loading on tariff fears in 2025 providing a temporary cushion thus far. Looking to 2026, we think these temporary benefits are set to unwind, with Maersk's equity up 22% in 2025 whilst freight rates are down -35%. We expect supply-demand dynamics to prevail as a record orderbook phases in and pressures earnings downwards; we are forecasting Ocean EBITDA to contract -58% YoY FY26e. Our estimates for FY26/FY27 EBITDA sit -6%/-8% below consensus (Visible Alpha), and we forecast Maersk to be Free Cash Flow negative for the next two years. Capex for fleet renewal investment, logistics investment and a renewed desire to buy back shares (should management chose to extend the programme beyond 2026) are further cash commitments. Valuation: Shares trade on 0.6x P/B vs. a through cycle multiple of 1.2x. This may screen as deep value, but we think impaired P/B is justified, given a lower forecasted outlook for return on assets. The ACI is an EU legal framework officially introduced in 2023 to provide the EU a tool to respond to third country “coercion” . In brief, coercion occurs when a third-country tries to force the EU or a member state to change policies via unjustified trade and/or financial tools (EU, 22-Nov- 23). Would implementing the ACI be slow? Yes. The framework has three phases: 1) examination, 2) dialogue and de-escalation, and 3) countermeasures. In the first phase the Commission investigates any third country measure to determine whether conditions are met for the ACI, with a 4- month non-binding deadline. If conditions are met, the Commission can then proceed with diplomatic talks. If these also fail, with a 3-month deadline (also non-binding), then the Commission drafts countermeasures. The Council must then approve the measures by a qualified majority voting. Can services be targeted? Yes, and we’re surprised that threat hasn’t been louder, or services not included in the package being considered. The retaliatory measures available range from tariffs and import restrictions, to restrictions on IP , financial and capital market access, public procurement and contract vetoes. records.text: Policy drag: Regulatory uncertainty has created significant challenges for the US wind power market, especially for offshore wind, with the Trump administration pausing federal leases for all large-scale offshore wind projects under construction. Early-stage projects may get cancelled: In our base case, we assume that about 25GW of later-stage projects currently in the pipeline (per BloombergNEF data) will accelerate development to meet the safe-harbor requirements (Figure 27) and reach completion before 2030. However, many early-stage projects are at risk of cancellation. Turbine OEMs have largely locked in production capacity for the next two years, limiting developers’ ability to place safe-harbor-compliant orders. In addition, wind projects typically face lengthy interconnection queues (Figure 10 on page 8). Bringing projects into service before the relevant deadline appears increasingly challenging. Outlook to 2035: We therefore expect limited growth in US wind power generation through 2030, followed by a stronger rebound as industry confidence return and policy clarity improves (Figure 28). Despite the near-term headwinds, the technology remains economically attractive relative to fossil-fuel counterparts (Figure 29). While we maintain our 'lower and later' assumption for aircraft production rates, which puts us 6% below consensus deliveries on average for FY26-30 (range -2-9%), our financial forecasts are more in line, as we think gross margin expansion due to mix, pricing power and production efficiencies are not accurately reflected in consensus. We also view the company as well placed to benefit from rising European defence spending, as well as increased shareholder returns, potentially via a buyback. In turn, this should increase market confidence in Airbus's medium-term potential, supporting a further rerating. Valuation: The stock now trades on 11x 2028e EV/EBIT (MSe), a 20% discount to the sector on 14x. While this is understandable given the recent disruption, we think the stock ultimately deserves a premium, given the operational momentum, upside potential, and higher capital returns in prospect. M Idea 6 Tax Refund Expectations Tax returns will start to be collected on January 26th, and refunds to consumers should start to ramp around mid-February. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) included many consumer tax credits and deductions that were retroactive to 2025 and therefore should boost tax refunds this year. Overall, we expect refunds to be $40-70bn higher this year than last, mostly due to these retroactive tax cuts. Taking the midpoint of this estimate, we expect total refunds by the end of May to total ~$350bn, about 20% higher than those of 2025. OBBBA effects on tax refunds Benefits from retroactive tax cuts in the OBBBA will be received through refunds this year. Last year's fiscal bill included many consumer-facing provisions that will affect individual tax rates and transfer payments. Many of the consumer tax cuts within the bill were frontloaded, beginning retroactively in fiscal year 2025 and ending in fiscal year 2028. The IRS announced last year that there would be no changes to individual withholding tables for 2025. As a result, consumers have not yet received the benefits from these tax cuts for the 2025 fiscal year; the retroactive provisions will be made up for when tax returns are filed. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 79 Software & Services SAP (SAP GY) Adam Wood Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €285/sh (Upside to PT: 41%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: SAP is the global leader in Enterprise Resource Planning software. After a standout 2024 (c. 72% total return), SAP derated through 2025 (with a -11% total return) as CCB growth moderated and as AI disruption debates weighed on investor sentiment. In 2026, we see an attractive valuation equation, from which we expect SAP to continue deliver mid-20s % organic cloud revenue growth, which will drive an overall group revenue growth acceleration in 2026 (12%+ y/y). Further productivity gains from investments in AI and automation should drive c. 15% operating profit growth on an ex-FX basis (non-IFRS operating margins increase to 29% from ~28% in our base case), while SAP's close to €4bn net cash position and strong FCF generation leaves a high likelihood of further capital returns via buybacks, driving EPS growth in the high-teens. Longer term, we see a clear pathway ahead to double EPS by 2030, driven by the continued shift to S/4HANA within SAP's €10bn+ maintenance installed base. Regarding AI, given the pullback in sector multiples, we think investors will take a more 'idiosyncratic' approach to the assessment of risks versus opportunities ahead for vendors from an agentic AI perspective. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 US Economics: Income, Spending, and Cohort Implications Higher refunds and lower tax rates will result in a boost in disposable personal income in 1Q. While we do not expect the same immediate jump in consumption, we do expect refunds and the bill as a whole to support consumption throughout the year. Income and spending Higher refunds should boost disposable income in 1Q. The BEA incorporates any expected tax changes into its personal income data in January of each year. As a result, even though tax refunds will not begin to be received until February, we expect to see the jump in personal income in January. Overall, we expect real disposable personal income to rise at a 4.1% annual rate in 1Q after running close to flat in 2H25. While refunds should also boost spending, we do not expect the same immediate jump in consumption. This is partly technical and partly due to how consumers typically use refunds. Since the increase in income will be recorded in January, but not actually received until February and beyond, we expect a large discrepancy between spending and income in January, and thus a spike in the saving rate. Even once consumers do begin to receive refunds in February, we still do not expect the same immediate effects on spending. In our AlphaWise Consumer Pulse survey, consumers have historically reported that the main two uses of tax refunds are saving and paying off debt, neither of which count as consumption. records.text: DP. We expect Prime Minister Takaichi's intentions to be strongly reflected in fiscal/economic policy, national security/diplomacy, as well as greater momentum in policy implementation. Regarding the market impact, it is a well-known anomaly that share prices tend to rise after the Lower House dissolution until the election. The general trend after an election is that if the leading party in the ruling coalition wins a majority on its own, share prices continue to rise, but if it fails to win a majority, momentum declines (Exhibit 4). Of note, after the 2005 Lower House election under former Prime Minister Koizumi and the 2012 Lower House election in which the LDP led by former Prime Minister Abe took power, the establishment of a long-term administration led to a prolonged rise in share prices (Exhibit 5). Looking at factor returns after an election, if the leading party in the ruling coalition wins a majority on its own, we think that investors will show a preference for large-cap stocks with strong earnings/high beta. If the leading party in the ruling coalition fails to win a majority on its own, we expect undervalued stocks and those with high dividend yields to become relatively more performative (Exhibit 6).

For more on the ACI, see our previous analysis here. 3/ Does the EU still fear US ‘escalation dominance’? The EU did not use the ACI in response to last year’s US tariffs. As we detailed in Friday’s note, the EU has certain points of economic leverage over the US. The EU dominates chemical (including pharma) imports into the US, for example. The Single Market is also a significant market for US exports. Restrict ing access would be costly to the US and is possible under the ACI . But the US has leverage too. The US dominates tech service imports into Europe and has an increasingly significant role in European energy imports. We also know from how President Trump reacted to other countries who pushed back last year that if the EU retaliates, the US will too, and the costs could quickly rise for both sides. 4/ Ukraine security a constraint on EU response. However, as it takes time for such developments to appear in the actual CPI statistics, communication for the time being is expected to rely on corporate surveys conducted by the BoJ regional branches and headquarters and data related to inflation expectations (Exhibit 7 ). Although some underlying inflation indicators are originally designed to capture the interaction between wages and prices (for example, the trend component of the CPI for services), at this stage they show only a temporary leveling-off followed by a slight expansion in the pace of increase ( Exhibit 8 ). records.text: 30 South Africa: Political narrative to move toward leadership succession COUNTRY VIEWS ANC National Conference: This five-yearly event, scheduled for December 2027, is the party’s highest-level and largest decision-making body for electing new leadership and setting policy. As the ANC no longer has a legislative majority, the conference might mandate Cyril Ramaphosa to stay in office as national president and head of the GNU until he steps down in 2029. His relative popularity as a political leader supports this assumption, despite the ANC’s national support slipping below 40% in some early polling. Growth, the ANC’s existential priority: The GNU is the only political compromise that can support the state’s ‘Operation Vulindlela’ structural reform unit and ongoing urgent official action to remove the binding constraints on growth by mobilising private investment in key infrastructure, in our view. This policy began in Q3 2020, and we expect tangible results to start arriving from H2 2027. This is evidenced in our GDP forecasts, which climb to 1.9% by 2027 from 1.6% this year and 1.2% in 2025. Whether the policy will be enough to impact ANC voter support will be revealed by the outcome of the pivotal 2029 national and provincial elections. 20/01/2026 Early opinion polling* shows the ANC national support below 40% while the DA climbs 37% 32% 8% 7% 6% 0% 20% 40% African National Congress (ANC) Democratic Alliance (DA) uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) Inkath

In a scenario where the full upside in European prices and margins materialises – reflecting a higher through-the-cycle price floor and utilization-driven margin uplift, as outlined in our New Clearing Price framework – ArcelorMittal’s valuation would compress to ~3.9x EV/EBITDA, versus a historical through-the-cycle multiple of ~7.1x. While each measure released so far has been mild, we believe this is important for the market as we expect more measures to be rolled out and market expectations were low. The fall in the number of newborns is likely to invite some policy reactions as it likely surprised on the downside. While it is likely that more measures such as subsidies will be taken, they will not likely be aggressive enough to change the trajectory as effectively as the change in GDP . The number of newborns (7.92mn in 2025, 1.6mn below 2024) is often treated as an independent variable which affects the economy in the long run. But we think the relationship is more complicated than that. When the economy is in deflation and youth unemployment high on a persistent basis, the number of newborns will be affected which in turn affects the economy. This is why the importance of maintaining growth stability goes beyond short term growth and inflation. We see risks to our 2026 forecast tilted towards the upside. The decline in wireless telephone services especially should not reflect government shutdown measurement issues, as this is one of just a few components that was able to be calculated for October. In the past (notably March 2017), this component has experienced large one-time changes based on the quality adjustment process. For example, as wireless plans include more features for the same price, the effective quality-adjusted price declines. One-time quality adjustments or lack of available data (unrelated to shutdown issues) could be the more likely cause of sizeable price changes in these components. The ACI has never been used but is the EU’s broadest and, potentially, most powerful tool (Exhibit 3). Three steps are required to activate the ACI. First, the European Commission would declare the existence of economic coercion and propose activation of the ACI. Second, the EU Council would need to approve the Commission’s proposal by qualified majority (requiring the support of 55% of member states representing at least 65% of the EU population) within 10 weeks. Then the EU Commission would have up to 6 months to deploy its response measures, following a non-binding consultation with relevant economic stakeholders and EU institutions. The implementation of these measures would likely be delayed by a flexible and potentially long period. This flexibility is a key aspect of its deployment since it allows both to signal potential EU action and to allow time for negotiation. The ACI could allow the EU to impose tariffs on services imports from the US (Exhibit 4, left). For reference, a flat 10% tariff on all EU imports of US services could mechanically raise about EUR 50bn in revenues. records.text: ects (If you build it, AI will come, 17 October, 2025). We think that AI has kept the US economy out of recession. In How will immigration and AI impact the neutral rate?, November 20, 2017 - we noted the stronger productivity associated with a widespread use of AI can put sharp upward pressure on the neutral rate over time. Additionally, we noted that Fed policymakers will also be attentive to the labor market if labor slack increases due to worker replacement or augmentation from AI. And in this case, even when the neutral rate is perceived to be higher, the Fed could cut rates to support the employment side of its mandate. We see two scenarios that US rates market can price: Scenario 1: The AI continued boom scenario: a twist steepener? In this scenario, one can assume that AI investment continues unabated into 2026, propping growth and productivity, and raising the perceived neutral rate, while also negatively affects parts of labor market. In this scenario we could see the market price a higher long term neutral, and high issuance (to fund AI projects) in the long-end – alongside a dovish Fed accounting for the Fed’s recent imbalanced reaction function - adding a bear or twist steepening risk to the curve. records.text: 6 Limits to near-term load growth: The US grid has limited capacity to absorb more load (highlighted by low reserve margins) and faces obstacles to a rapid increase in generation capacity, highlighted by long interconnection queues. This has no easy fix, in our view. Reserve margins are low: An April 2025 study by the NERC on the US power system estimated the average reserve margin – which measures the extra electrical generation a system has beyond its expected peak demand and is a crucial buffer against unexpected outages or demand spikes – at about 20%. In ERCOT, Texas, one of the hotspots for US data center development, the system peaked at 118% of this capacity in summer 2024 (Figure 7). The NERC also calculated a ‘reference reserve margin’ – the threshold margin established by the state, provincial authority, ISO/regional transmission organization (RTO), or other regulatory body to provide the level of resources needed to meet standard reliability criteria (e.g. to keep loss-of-load expectation below one day in 10 years). The NERC put the level at between 10–20%, depending on the state. We define 10% as the minimum sustainable reserve margin in our analysis. Given the above numbers, we cannot assume the reserve margin can decline by much without causing system-reliability issues, particularly in periods of low renewable generation. records.text: 4 Rising electricity prices create political headache: US data center project pipelines continued to surge in 2025, with the most growth seen in committed and early-stage projects, particularly in Virginia, Texas, and Georgia (Figure 2). Meanwhile, broader electrification, including growth in electric vehicles and heat pumps, alongside efforts to reshore manufacturing, should further lift overall power demand and prices. According to EIA data, US electricity bills rose 6% y/y in October 2025 across sectors nationwide. In some states (e.g. Illinois and Pennsylvania), price increases have been even sharper (Figure 3). Even if one assumes developers can afford them, we see surging power prices as a growing political headwind for data center expansion, particularly with US mid-term elections scheduled for 3 November. A patchwork of regulations: In July 2025, an executive order from US President Donald Trump streamlined permitting for large-scale data centers on federal land, enabling faster approvals. That said, associated infrastructure – e.g. transmission lines – often crosses non-federal land and is still subject to state-level approval. Several states are seeking to address the energy implications of rapid data center expansion. Backed by high approval ratings, this move will test her "responsible, expansionary fiscal policy." A decisive victory would solidify her power base, leading markets to anticipate fiscal expansion and deregulation, likely driving stocks higher an d weakening the yen. This political landscape heavily influences monetary policy. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 0.75% in December, and we forecast the next hike for April. However, a strong election mandate for fiscal expansion could increase political pressure on the BoJ to delay further hikes. Conversely, a weakening yen could accelerate the pace of tightening. The uniform response of EU leaders suggests that retaliation is more likely than n last year if Trump decides to move forward with new tariffs. At the same time, we would expect the EU’s retaliation approach to proceed gradually to leave room for de-escalation. We therefore expect the EU to start by pausing the implementation of the EU-US trade deal and readying counter-tariffs to be implemented shortly after any US tariff increases. In addition, we expect the EU to activate the ACI if the US escalates tensions further, but without implementing any measures immediately to leave additional time for negotiation.
